title: The Jungle, the 1906 food laws and the FDA (1906)

steps.claim: Upton Sinclair's The Jungle is published by Doubleday, Page

test.source: Doubleday, Page & Co. trade edition, February 26, 1906; serialized in Appeal to Reason from February 25, 1905

steps.note: The Jungle was a novel about immigrant workers in Chicago's meatpacking plants. Sinclair wrote it to expose how the men were treated; readers fixed instead on what he described going into the sausage: rats, poisoned bread, workers who fell into rendering vats. 'I aimed at the public's heart,' he said, 'and by accident I hit it in the stomach.' Within four months Congress had passed two food laws, and the agency that enforced one of them grew into the FDA.

steps.claim: Claim: The Jungle got the pure-food bill through the Senate

test.source: The book's publication, February 26, 1906; the Senate had passed Heyburn's pure-food bill (S. 88) on February 21, 1906, 63–4

steps.note: Dated when the claimed cause arrived; tested against the Senate vote. Harvey Wiley's Bureau of Chemistry had pushed a pure-food law since the 1880s and the Senate passed it five days before the book came out. The book moved the House, where the bill had died for years; it did not move the Senate. Busted as the origin, plausible as the finisher.

steps.claim: Senator Beveridge's meat-inspection amendment passes the Senate without a dissenting vote

test.source: Senate adoption of the Beveridge amendment to the Agricultural Appropriation bill, May 25, 1906

steps.link_why: Beveridge wrote the amendment after reading the book and meeting Sinclair; Roosevelt backed it (Beveridge's correspondence, in Claude Bowers's 1932 biography)

steps.claim: Roosevelt sends the Neill–Reynolds report on the Chicago packinghouses to Congress

test.source: Presidential message transmitting the Neill–Reynolds Report, June 4, 1906 (H. Doc. 873, 59th Cong.)

steps.link_why: Roosevelt commissioned Charles Neill and James Reynolds in March 1906 to test Sinclair's account, and told Congress their findings confirmed it

steps.claim: The Federal Meat Inspection Act is signed

test.source: Pub. L. 59-382, 34 Stat. 674, signed June 30, 1906

steps.link_why: the House conferees gave way after the Neill–Reynolds report; Roosevelt's own account credits the report, and the report credits the book

steps.claim: The Pure Food and Drug Act is signed the same day

test.source: Pub. L. 59-384, 34 Stat. 768, signed June 30, 1906

steps.link_why: the House passed the long-stalled bill on June 23, 1906, in the month of the meat scandal; historians (Oscar Anderson, James Harvey Young) credit the uproar with breaking the House deadlock

steps.claim: The enforcement bureau is renamed the Food and Drug Administration

test.source: Agricultural Appropriation Act for fiscal 1931, approved May 27, 1930, shortened 'Food, Drug, and Insecticide Administration' to 'Food and Drug Administration'

steps.link_why: the agency's own history: the Bureau of Chemistry enforced the 1906 Act, was split into a regulatory arm in 1927 and renamed in 1930

steps.claim: Elixir Sulfanilamide kills more than 100 people; the 1906 Act lets the FDA act only on mislabeling

test.source: The American Medical Association is told of the Tulsa deaths on October 11, 1937; FDA field investigation follows; 107 deaths by the FDA's count

steps.link_why: the FDA's report to Congress (November 1937) said it could seize the elixir only because it was misbranded, not because it was poisonous

steps.claim: The Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act replaces the 1906 law and requires proof of safety before sale

test.source: Pub. L. 75-717, 52 Stat. 1040, signed June 25, 1938

steps.link_why: the bill had stalled since 1933; the elixir deaths carried it (Senate Report 152, 75th Cong.; Wallace Janssen's FDA history)
wiki: Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act

title: The Triangle fire, the Factory Commission and the New Deal (1911)

steps.claim: Fire sweeps the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory in Greenwich Village; 146 workers die

test.source: Asch Building, Washington Place, New York, Saturday March 25, 1911; 146 dead, most of them young immigrant women

steps.note: The Triangle Waist Company made women's blouses on the top three floors of a ten-story building. When fire broke out, one stairway door was locked to stop theft, the fire escape collapsed and the firemen's ladders reached only the sixth floor. Dozens jumped. A crowd in Washington Square watched them fall; among the watchers was Frances Perkins, who would later run the US Department of Labor and call that afternoon 'the day the New Deal began'.

steps.claim: Rose Schneiderman tells a memorial meeting at the Metropolitan Opera House that 'the only way is through a strong working-class movement'

test.source: Metropolitan Opera House meeting called by the Women's Trade Union League, April 2, 1911

steps.link_why: the meeting was called for the fire's victims; her speech is in the next day's papers

steps.claim: Some 100,000 march in the rain behind the unidentified dead; 300,000 line the route

test.source: Funeral procession for the seven unidentified victims, April 5, 1911 (New York Times, April 6, 1911)

steps.link_why: the ILGWU and WTUL organized the procession as a protest

steps.claim: New York creates the Factory Investigating Commission, with Robert Wagner as chair and Al Smith as vice-chair

test.source: Chapter 561, Laws of New York 1911, signed June 30, 1911

steps.link_why: the Commission's own first report (1912) opens with the fire; Perkins, who ran its investigations, called it the fire's direct result

steps.claim: The Triangle owners are acquitted of manslaughter

test.source: People v. Harris and Blanck, verdict December 27, 1911

steps.link_why: the trial turned on whether the owners knew the ninth-floor door was locked; the acquittal fed the case for prevention by law rather than prosecution after the fact

steps.claim: New York's 54-hour law limits the week for women and children in factories

test.source: New York 54-hour bill, passed on the last night of the 1912 session, March 29–30, 1912; Perkins lobbied it through as the Consumers' League's agent

steps.link_why: Perkins's own account (The Roosevelt I Knew; her Columbia oral history) ties the bill's passage to the political weather after the fire

steps.claim: The Commission's bills rewrite New York's labor code: by 1914 the legislature has passed 36 of them, on sprinklers, exits, hours, sanitation and child labor

test.reason: thirty-six separate statutes over three sessions, without a single enactment date; the Commission's reports (1912–1915) list them

steps.link_why: the Commission reported every bill as the fire's legacy; its reports are the record

steps.claim: Frances Perkins is sworn in as Secretary of Labor, the first woman in a US cabinet

test.source: Sworn in March 4, 1933, in Franklin Roosevelt's first cabinet

steps.link_why: Perkins herself: 'The New Deal began on March 25, 1911, the day the Triangle factory burned' (1964 lecture); Smith and Wagner carried the Commission's program into national politics

steps.claim: The Social Security Act is signed

test.source: Pub. L. 74-271, 49 Stat. 620, signed August 14, 1935

steps.link_why: Perkins chaired the Committee on Economic Security that wrote it; Wagner introduced it in the Senate

steps.claim: The Fair Labor Standards Act sets a federal minimum wage, a 44-hour week and limits on child labor

test.source: Pub. L. 75-718, 52 Stat. 1060, signed June 25, 1938

steps.link_why: Perkins had made a wage-and-hour law her condition for taking the job in 1933; her biographer Kirstin Downey and historian David Von Drehle (Triangle, 2003) draw the line from the Commission to the Act

title: Black Sunday, the Soil Conservation Act and the NRCS (1935)

steps.claim: Black Sunday: a dust storm a thousand miles wide turns day to night across the southern plains

test.source: Sunday April 14, 1935, Oklahoma and Texas panhandles, Kansas, Colorado; the AP's Robert Geiger wrote 'the dust bowl' the next day

steps.note: Through the early 1930s drought and plowed-up grassland produced dust storms across Oklahoma, Texas, Kansas and Colorado, the region a reporter named the Dust Bowl. The worst single storm came on Sunday April 14, 1935, when a front pushed a wall of black dust across the plains. It gave the crisis its name, and within two weeks Congress had created a permanent soil-conservation agency.

steps.claim: Claim: Black Sunday's dust blew into Hugh Bennett's Senate hearing and passed the Act

test.source: Black Sunday, April 14, 1935; Bennett's testimony to the Senate Public Lands Committee is dated April 2, 1935 in the NRCS's own history

steps.note: Dated when the claimed cause arrived; tested against the hearing. The story is that dust darkened Washington as Bennett spoke. His testimony was twelve days before Black Sunday, and the dust that reached the East in 1935 came from a March storm. The storm that named the Dust Bowl was not the one in the hearing room. Busted as told; the hearing and the dusty spring did the work together.

steps.claim: Claim: the Dust Bowl created federal soil conservation

test.source: Black Sunday, April 14, 1935; the Soil Erosion Service was set up in the Interior Department on September 19, 1933, with Bennett as chief

steps.note: Dated when the claimed cause arrived; tested against the Soil Erosion Service's creation. Bennett had a federal agency and $5 million of public-works money eighteen months before Black Sunday. The storm made it permanent; it did not start it.

steps.claim: The Soil Conservation Act creates the Soil Conservation Service in the Department of Agriculture

test.source: Pub. L. 74-46, 49 Stat. 163, signed April 27, 1935

steps.link_why: the Act's preamble names 'the wastage of soil and moisture resources' as 'a menace to the national welfare'; the NRCS history and Donald Worster (Dust Bowl, 1979) tie its speed to the spring storms

steps.claim: After the Supreme Court strikes down the AAA, Congress pays farmers to plant soil-conserving crops

test.source: Soil Conservation and Domestic Allotment Act, Pub. L. 74-461, signed February 29, 1936, after United States v. Butler (January 6, 1936)

steps.link_why: Congress rewrote the farm program as conservation to survive the Court; the SCS's new standing made that possible (Worster; the Act's own text)
wiki: Soil Conservation and Domestic Allotment Act of 1936

steps.claim: Roosevelt sends every governor a model law for local soil conservation districts

test.source: President's letter to the governors transmitting the Standard State Soil Conservation Districts Law, February 27, 1937

steps.link_why: the letter cites the plains' erosion and asks the states to give farmers a local body to work with the SCS

steps.claim: The first soil conservation district is organized at Brown Creek, North Carolina, in Bennett's home county

test.source: Brown Creek Soil Conservation District, Anson County, NC, August 4, 1937

steps.link_why: organized under North Carolina's version of the model law; today nearly 3,000 districts cover almost all US farmland (NACD)

steps.claim: The Soil Conservation Service becomes the Natural Resources Conservation Service

test.source: Federal Crop Insurance Reform and Department of Agriculture Reorganization Act of 1994, Pub. L. 103-354, signed October 13, 1994; the new name took effect October 20, 1994

steps.link_why: the same agency, renamed; its field offices still sit in the districts the 1937 model law created

title: Sputnik, NASA, the Education Act and ARPA (1957)

steps.claim: The Soviet Union launches Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite

test.source: Launched from Baikonur, October 4, 1957 (19:28 UTC); 83.6 kg, orbit of about 96 minutes

steps.note: Sputnik was a polished metal sphere the size of a beach ball that beeped on a radio frequency amateurs could hear. The United States had assumed it would be first into space; it was not, and the rocket that carried Sputnik could plainly carry a warhead. In the year that followed, Washington created a research agency, a space agency and the first big federal program for schools.

steps.claim: Sputnik 2 carries the dog Laika into orbit

test.source: Launched November 3, 1957; 508 kg

steps.link_why: the second launch, six times heavier, ended the argument that the first was a stunt

steps.claim: The first US attempt, Vanguard TV-3, explodes on the pad on live television

test.source: Cape Canaveral, December 6, 1957; the press called it 'Flopnik' and 'Kaputnik'

steps.link_why: the Navy's launch was rushed forward in answer to Sputnik (Eisenhower's own account, Waging Peace)

steps.claim: Explorer 1 reaches orbit on an Army Jupiter-C and finds the Van Allen belts

test.source: Launched January 31, 1958, 10:48 p.m. EST, from Cape Canaveral

steps.link_why: von Braun's team was cleared to launch only after Vanguard failed

steps.claim: The Advanced Research Projects Agency is created inside the Pentagon

test.source: Department of Defense Directive 5105.15, February 7, 1958; funded by Pub. L. 85-325, February 12, 1958

steps.link_why: Secretary McElroy proposed it in November 1957 as the answer to the services' rival missile programs exposed by Sputnik; DARPA's own history says so

steps.claim: Eisenhower asks Congress for a civilian space agency

test.source: Special message to Congress on space science and exploration, April 2, 1958

steps.link_why: the message followed the President's Science Advisory Committee's recommendation (Killian), itself a Sputnik creation

steps.claim: The National Aeronautics and Space Act is signed

test.source: Pub. L. 85-568, 72 Stat. 426, signed July 29, 1958

steps.link_why: Lyndon Johnson's Senate Preparedness subcommittee hearings (from November 25, 1957) built the case; the Act's history opens with Sputnik

steps.claim: The National Defense Education Act puts federal money into science, math and language teaching and student loans

test.source: Pub. L. 85-864, 72 Stat. 1580, signed September 2, 1958

steps.link_why: the Act's title and findings speak of 'the present emergency'; its sponsors Lister Hill and Carl Elliott cited Sputnik on the floor

steps.claim: NASA opens for business, absorbing the NACA

test.source: NASA began operations October 1, 1958, with the NACA's 8,000 staff and three laboratories

steps.link_why: the Space Act's effective date

steps.claim: ARPA's network sends its first message between UCLA and SRI in Menlo Park

test.source: First ARPANET message, UCLA to SRI, October 29, 1969, 10:30 p.m.

steps.link_why: funded by ARPA's Information Processing Techniques Office (1962); the agency's existence is Sputnik's, the network's purpose was resource sharing, not nuclear survival (Hafner & Lyon, Where Wizards Stay Up Late)

title: Unsafe at Any Speed, NHTSA and the airbag (1965)

steps.claim: Ralph Nader publishes Unsafe at Any Speed

test.source: Grossman Publishers, November 30, 1965

steps.note: Unsafe at Any Speed was a young lawyer's book arguing that American cars killed people by design: dashboards that impaled, steering columns that speared, and a Chevrolet Corvair that could flip in a turn. Carmakers had blamed drivers. Within ten months Congress had passed the first federal safety standards for cars; the agency that writes them, the seat-belt law in your state and the airbag in your steering wheel all trace back to it.

steps.claim: General Motors' president apologizes to Nader before a Senate subcommittee for hiring detectives to investigate him

test.source: James Roche before the Senate Subcommittee on Executive Reorganization (Ribicoff), March 22, 1966

steps.link_why: GM's surveillance was of the book's author; the hearing made the book front-page news and Nader a national figure (Ribicoff's own statement that day)

steps.claim: The National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act is signed, with the Highway Safety Act

test.source: Pub. L. 89-563, 80 Stat. 718, and Pub. L. 89-564, signed September 9, 1966

steps.link_why: Johnson's signing statement; the Senate Commerce Committee report (S. Rep. 1301, 89th Cong.) and Nader's testimony of February 10, 1966
wiki: National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act

steps.claim: The first Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards are issued

test.source: Initial FMVSS 101–120 issued January 31, 1967, effective for 1968 model cars: seat belts at every seating position, energy-absorbing steering columns, padded dashboards

steps.link_why: the Act required standards within 15 months; the first set covers the book's chapters almost item by item

steps.claim: Claim: the book killed the Corvair

test.source: The book, November 30, 1965; Corvair sales had already fallen from about 300,000 (1962) to about 200,000 (1964) after the Ford Mustang arrived on April 17, 1964

steps.note: Dated when the claimed cause arrived; tested against the Mustang's launch, which began the Corvair's slide. GM had cut the car's development before the book and ended it in 1969. In 1972 a NHTSA study found the 1960–63 Corvair no more prone to roll over than its peers. Busted as the start of the decline; plausible as the end of it.

steps.claim: The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration is established

test.source: Highway Safety Act of 1970, Title II of Pub. L. 91-605, signed December 31, 1970; successor to the National Highway Safety Bureau of 1966

steps.link_why: the 1966 Act's bureau, given agency status; its first administrator, William Haddon, was the Ribicoff hearings' expert witness

steps.claim: The Supreme Court rules that scrapping the passive-restraint rule was arbitrary

test.source: Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Ass'n v. State Farm, 463 U.S. 29, decided June 24, 1983

steps.link_why: the rule at issue, FMVSS 208, was written under the 1966 Act; the Court held the agency had to explain why it dropped airbags
wiki: Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Ass'n v. State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Co.

steps.claim: Secretary Dole orders passive restraints from the 1987 models unless states covering two-thirds of the population pass seat-belt laws

test.source: Final rule on FMVSS 208, July 11, 1984 (49 FR 28962)

steps.link_why: the Department's response to State Farm; the rule's text says so

steps.claim: New York passes the first mandatory seat-belt law

test.source: Signed by Governor Cuomo July 12, 1984; in force December 1, 1984

steps.link_why: the state bill was moving before the Dole rule; carmakers then lobbied the other states to pass belt laws to escape the airbag mandate (the rule's own trade-off)
wiki: Seat belt laws in the United States

steps.claim: Congress requires airbags on both front seats of every new car

test.source: Intermodal Surface Transportation Efficiency Act, Pub. L. 102-240, signed December 18, 1991: driver and passenger airbags in all cars by model year 1998

steps.link_why: the statute ended the airbag-or-belt-law bargain of 1984; Nader's Center for Auto Safety was among the groups credited in the floor debate

title: The Cuyahoga fire, Earth Day, the EPA and the Clean Water Act (1969)

steps.claim: Oil and debris on the Cuyahoga River catch fire in Cleveland

test.source: Sunday June 22, 1969, about noon, near the Republic Steel works; out in under 30 minutes; about $50,000 in damage to two rail bridges

steps.note: The Cuyahoga runs through Cleveland's steel district into Lake Erie, and for a century it was an open sewer for oil and industrial waste. On June 22, 1969, sparks from a train set the slick on fire. The blaze was small and out in half an hour; no one photographed it. But the river had burned before, and when Time magazine ran a 1952 photo of it ablaze the story became a symbol of what American rivers had come to.

steps.claim: Time's 'America's Sewage System and the Price of Optimism' makes the river a national symbol, with a photo of the 1952 fire

test.source: Time, August 1, 1969

steps.link_why: the article is about the June fire; the photograph is of the November 1952 one (Cleveland Press archive)

steps.claim: The National Environmental Policy Act is signed on New Year's Day

test.source: Pub. L. 91-190, 83 Stat. 852, signed January 1, 1970

steps.link_why: Senator Jackson's bill predates the fire; Nixon's signing statement spoke of the 'environmental decade', and the river was one of its stock examples

steps.claim: The first Earth Day draws some 20 million Americans

test.source: April 22, 1970; Senator Gaylord Nelson announced the teach-in in Seattle on September 20, 1969

steps.link_why: Earth Day organizers used the river as an emblem; Nelson's own account credits Santa Barbara
steps.note: Nelson said the idea came to him after the Santa Barbara oil spill of January 1969, not the Cuyahoga; the burning river was on the posters all the same. Ordered after the fire, as it was; caused by it, not shown.

steps.claim: The Environmental Protection Agency opens

test.source: Reorganization Plan No. 3 of 1970, sent to Congress July 9, 1970; EPA began operations December 2, 1970 under William Ruckelshaus

steps.link_why: Nixon's message on the reorganization plan; Ruckelshaus's first enforcement actions, within a week of opening, targeted Cleveland, Detroit and Atlanta for sewage

steps.claim: The Clean Air Act of 1970 is signed

test.source: Pub. L. 91-604, 84 Stat. 1676, signed December 31, 1970

steps.link_why: Muskie's bill rode the same year's wave; the river is the water-side companion, not the cause

steps.claim: The United States and Canada sign the Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement

test.source: Signed in Ottawa by Nixon and Trudeau, April 15, 1972

steps.link_why: Lake Erie, which the Cuyahoga feeds, was the agreement's declared emergency (the IJC's 1970 report)

steps.claim: Congress overrides Nixon's veto to pass the Clean Water Act

test.source: Federal Water Pollution Control Act Amendments of 1972, Pub. L. 92-500, enacted over the veto October 18, 1972

steps.link_why: the burning river is in the Senate debate and in Muskie's committee report; the Act's goal of 'fishable, swimmable' waters by 1983 was written against examples like it

steps.claim: Ohio lifts the fish-consumption restriction on the lower Cuyahoga

test.reason: a state agency announcement in March 2019 that I cannot date to the day

steps.link_why: Ohio EPA and the US EPA Great Lakes National Program Office credit the Clean Water Act permits on the river's dischargers
steps.note: Fifty years on, Ohio EPA removed the 'fish consumption' impairment from the river's Area of Concern listing; the river is not yet delisted.

steps.claim: New York's health commissioner declares a health emergency at Love Canal and tells pregnant women and small children to leave

test.source: Commissioner Robert Whalen's order, August 2, 1978, covering the first two rings of houses on 97th and 99th Streets, Niagara Falls

steps.note: Love Canal was a neighborhood in Niagara Falls, New York, built on and around a canal that Hooker Chemical had filled with some 21,000 tons of chemical waste and then sold to the school board for a dollar in 1953. By the 1970s the drums were surfacing, basements smelled, and residents counted miscarriages and birth defects. The evacuation that began in August 1978 led to the federal law that pays to clean up abandoned toxic sites.

steps.claim: Lois Gibbs forms the Love Canal Homeowners Association

test.source: Founded August 4, 1978, two days after the state order

steps.link_why: Gibbs, whose son attended the school on the canal, organized the residents the order left out

steps.claim: President Carter declares a federal emergency, the first for a man-made disaster

test.source: Federal emergency declaration, August 7, 1978; the state bought the 239 homes in the first two rings

steps.link_why: the declaration followed the state's request after Whalen's order

steps.claim: After an EPA chromosome study, residents hold two EPA officials for five hours

test.source: Picciano chromosome study released May 17, 1980; residents detain two EPA officials on May 19, 1980

steps.link_why: the Homeowners Association acted after the study showed chromosome damage in 11 of 36 residents and the government had still not moved the rest

steps.claim: Carter orders the remaining 700 families relocated

test.source: Second federal emergency declaration, May 21, 1980; permanent relocation funded October 1, 1980

steps.link_why: two days after the hostage incident, which the White House's own statements acknowledged

steps.claim: The Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act (Superfund) is signed

test.source: Pub. L. 96-510, 94 Stat. 2767, signed December 11, 1980, in the lame-duck session

steps.link_why: Carter's signing remarks; the Senate Environment Committee's report (S. Rep. 96-848) and the EPA's 1979 legislative proposal both lead with Love Canal

steps.claim: Love Canal is on the first National Priorities List

test.source: First NPL, 406 sites, published 48 FR 40658, September 8, 1983

steps.link_why: the list the Act required; Love Canal was the test case for the hazard ranking system

steps.claim: Congress reauthorizes Superfund at $8.5 billion and adds the community right-to-know law

test.source: Superfund Amendments and Reauthorization Act, Pub. L. 99-499, signed October 17, 1986; Title III is the Emergency Planning and Community Right-to-Know Act

steps.link_why: the reauthorization of the 1980 Act; Title III followed the Bhopal release of December 1984
wiki: Superfund Amendments and Reauthorization Act of 1986

steps.claim: Occidental, Hooker's parent, settles the federal cleanup claim for $129 million

test.reason: a consent decree in December 1995 that I cannot date to the day

steps.link_why: United States v. Occidental Chemical Corp. (W.D.N.Y.), a CERCLA cost-recovery action
steps.note: Occidental had settled with New York for $98 million in June 1994. The federal case was brought under CERCLA's liability sections.

steps.claim: The EPA deletes Love Canal from the National Priorities List

test.source: Notice of deletion, 69 FR 58328, September 30, 2004

steps.link_why: the Act's own end-state for a site; about 260 of the homes were resold as Black Creek Village

title: Three Mile Island, the Kemeny Commission and the long pause (1979)

steps.claim: Three Mile Island Unit 2 suffers a partial meltdown

test.source: 4:00 a.m., March 28, 1979, Londonderry Township, Pennsylvania; a stuck-open relief valve and misread instruments uncovered the core

steps.note: Three Mile Island was a two-reactor nuclear plant on the Susquehanna River near Harrisburg. Early on March 28, 1979, a valve stuck open in Unit 2 and the operators, misreading their gauges, shut off the emergency cooling. About half the core melted. Little radiation escaped and no one was shown to have been hurt, but for five days the country did not know that, and the film The China Syndrome had opened twelve days earlier. It was the worst accident in US commercial nuclear history.

steps.claim: Governor Thornburgh advises pregnant women and preschool children within five miles to leave

test.source: Advisory issued March 30, 1979; about 140,000 people left the area

steps.link_why: the advisory followed an uncontrolled release that morning and the NRC's confused advice (the Kemeny report's narrative)

steps.claim: Carter creates the Kemeny Commission

test.source: Executive Order 12130, April 11, 1979; John Kemeny, president of Dartmouth, chair

steps.link_why: the order's text: to investigate the accident at Three Mile Island
wiki: President's Commission on the Accident at Three Mile Island

steps.claim: The Kemeny report finds 'fundamental changes' are needed in the industry and the NRC

test.source: Report of the President's Commission on the Accident at Three Mile Island, delivered October 30, 1979

steps.link_why: the Commission's own charge; it recommended abolishing the five-member NRC for a single administrator, operator training standards and emergency planning

steps.claim: Carter accepts most of the report and gives FEMA the lead on off-site emergency planning

test.source: President's statement on the Kemeny Commission report, December 7, 1979

steps.link_why: the statement answers the report point by point; the industry's Institute of Nuclear Power Operations, formed that month, answered its training findings

steps.claim: The NRC requires approved emergency plans within ten miles of every plant as a condition of a license

test.source: Final rule on emergency planning, 10 CFR 50.47 and Appendix E, 45 FR 55402, August 19, 1980

steps.link_why: the rule's preamble cites the accident and the Kemeny and Rogovin reports; it is why Shoreham, finished in 1984, never ran

steps.claim: Claim: Three Mile Island stopped US reactor orders

test.source: The accident, March 28, 1979; US utilities ordered 41 reactors in 1973, four in 1976, two in 1978 and none afterwards; every order placed after 1974 was later canceled (EIA)

steps.note: Dated when the claimed cause arrived; tested against the last order. Orders had fallen to nothing before the accident, on cost overruns, interest rates and flat demand after 1973. The accident kept them at nothing. Busted as the start; plausible as the lock.

steps.claim: No new reactor is licensed for 33 years, until the NRC approves Vogtle 3 and 4

test.source: NRC vote 4–1 to issue combined licenses for Vogtle Units 3 and 4, February 9, 2012; the first construction approval since 1978

steps.link_why: the NRC's own count; Chairman Jaczko's dissent cited Fukushima, the new gap-maker

steps.claim: Three Mile Island Unit 1 shuts down

test.source: Exelon shut down TMI-1 on September 20, 2019, for lack of a Pennsylvania subsidy

steps.link_why: economics, not safety: the plant had lost money against shale gas since 2015 (Exelon's filings)

steps.claim: Constellation agrees to restart Unit 1 to power Microsoft's data centers

test.source: Constellation announcement, September 20, 2024; 20-year power purchase agreement; renamed Crane Clean Energy Center

steps.link_why: the company's own announcement names the plant and the 2019 closure
wiki: Three Mile Island Nuclear Generating Station

title: The Exxon Valdez and the Oil Pollution Act (1989)

steps.claim: The tanker Exxon Valdez runs aground on Bligh Reef in Prince William Sound and spills about 11 million gallons of crude

test.source: 12:04 a.m. Alaska time, March 24, 1989; 10.8 million gallons by Exxon's count, up to 32 million by others

steps.note: The Exxon Valdez was a 987-foot tanker that left the Alaska pipeline terminal at Valdez on the night of March 23, 1989, strayed out of the shipping lane to avoid ice and hit a charted reef. Her single hull tore open and oil spread along 1,300 miles of shoreline, killing hundreds of thousands of seabirds and thousands of otters. It was the worst oil spill in US waters until Deepwater Horizon, and it broke a fourteen-year deadlock in Congress over oil-spill law.

steps.claim: Exxon's chairman apologizes in full-page newspaper ads

test.source: Lawrence Rawl's open letter, published April 3, 1989, in 166 newspapers

steps.link_why: the letter is about the spill; Rawl's absence from Alaska in the first days became the case study in crisis mishandling

steps.claim: Claim: the Exxon Valdez created the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund

test.source: The spill, March 24, 1989; the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund was created by the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1986, Pub. L. 99-509, October 21, 1986, but Congress never authorized its tax or its use

steps.note: Dated when the claimed cause arrived; tested against the fund's creation. The fund existed on paper for two and a half years before the spill. The Oil Pollution Act of 1990 gave it a five-cent-a-barrel tax and a purpose. Busted as the origin; the spill made it real.

steps.claim: Captain Hazelwood is convicted of negligent discharge of oil, a misdemeanor, and acquitted of the felonies

test.source: State of Alaska v. Hazelwood, Anchorage jury verdict, March 22, 1990

steps.link_why: the trial of the ship's master for the grounding

steps.claim: The Oil Pollution Act of 1990 is signed

test.source: Pub. L. 101-380, 104 Stat. 484, signed August 18, 1990

steps.link_why: the conference report (H. Rep. 101-653) and the floor statements of Senators Stevens and Mitchell open with the spill; the bill had been stuck between House and Senate since 1975 over whether to pre-empt state liability laws

steps.claim: Exxon pleads guilty to four misdemeanors and settles with the United States and Alaska for $1.025 billion

test.source: Plea agreement and civil consent decree approved by Judge Russel Holland, October 8, 1991: $25 million criminal fine, $100 million restitution, $900 million civil settlement over ten years

steps.link_why: the government's case for the spill; the civil money funded the Exxon Valdez Oil Spill Trustee Council

steps.claim: An Anchorage jury awards $5 billion in punitive damages to fishermen and natives

test.source: In re the Exxon Valdez, D. Alaska, jury verdict September 16, 1994

steps.link_why: the class action of about 32,000 plaintiffs harmed by the spill

steps.claim: The Supreme Court cuts the punitive award to about $507 million

test.source: Exxon Shipping Co. v. Baker, 554 U.S. 471, decided June 25, 2008: punitive damages in maritime cases capped at the compensatory award

steps.link_why: the same case, nineteen years after the spill; the opinion's one-to-one ratio is now the maritime rule

steps.claim: Single-hull tankers are barred from US waters

test.source: OPA 90 §4115, 46 U.S.C. §3703a: the phase-out schedule ends January 1, 2015 for all single-hull tank vessels; the IMO followed with MARPOL Regulation 13F in 1992

steps.link_why: the Act's own schedule, written against the Exxon Valdez's single hull; the National Research Council (1991) estimated a double hull would have cut her spill by more than half

title: The McDonald's coffee case and tort reform (1994)

steps.claim: An Albuquerque jury awards Stella Liebeck $2.86 million against McDonald's for coffee burns

test.source: Liebeck v. McDonald's Restaurants, Bernalillo County District Court, verdict August 18, 1994: $200,000 compensatory (reduced to $160,000 for her 20% fault) and $2.7 million punitive

steps.note: On February 27, 1992, Stella Liebeck, 79, spilled a cup of McDonald's coffee in her lap in a parked car and suffered third-degree burns over six percent of her body, needing skin grafts. She asked McDonald's for her medical costs, about $20,000; it offered $800. At trial the jury heard that the coffee was held at 180–190°F and that McDonald's had more than 700 prior burn complaints. The verdict became the most famous lawsuit in America, usually told wrong, and the emblem of a campaign to limit damage awards.

steps.claim: The judge cuts the punitive award to $480,000; the parties then settle for an undisclosed sum

test.source: Judge Robert Scott's order reducing punitive damages to three times compensatory, September 14, 1994; confidential settlement before appeal, December 1994

steps.link_why: the same case; the reduction is the part of the story the jokes leave out

steps.claim: The House passes the Contract with America's product-liability bill

test.source: H.R. 956, Common Sense Product Liability Legal Reform Act, passed the House March 10, 1995, 265–161

steps.link_why: sponsors and the American Tort Reform Association cited the coffee verdict in debate and in advertising as the model of a runaway jury

steps.claim: Claim: the Liebeck verdict started the tort-reform movement

test.source: The verdict, August 18, 1994; California's Medical Injury Compensation Reform Act capped non-economic damages at $250,000 on September 23, 1975, and the American Tort Reform Association was founded in 1986

steps.note: Dated when the claimed cause arrived; tested against MICRA. Damage caps were nineteen years old and the lobby eight when the coffee spilled. The case gave the movement its anecdote, not its start. Busted as origin; it is plainly the campaign's best-known exhibit (HBO's Hot Coffee, 2011, documents its use).

steps.claim: Seinfeld's Kramer sues over a spilled coffee

test.source: Seinfeld, 'The Maestro', NBC, October 5, 1995

steps.link_why: the episode's writers took the premise from the news coverage of the case; it fixed the popular version

steps.claim: Clinton vetoes the product-liability bill

test.source: Veto of H.R. 956, May 2, 1996; the House override failed May 9, 1996

steps.link_why: the same bill; the fight moved to the states

steps.claim: Texas caps non-economic damages in medical cases at $250,000

test.source: Texas House Bill 4, 78th Legislature, signed June 11, 2003; Proposition 12 amended the state constitution to protect the cap on September 13, 2003

steps.link_why: Texans for Lawsuit Reform's campaign and the Proposition 12 advertising used the coffee case; the bill's own findings speak of 'excessive' awards, not of coffee

steps.claim: The Class Action Fairness Act moves large class actions into federal court

test.source: Pub. L. 109-2, 119 Stat. 4, signed February 18, 2005

steps.link_why: the first federal tort-reform statute to pass after the 1996 veto; the coffee case is in the Senate debate as the stock example of a jackpot verdict

steps.claim: Claim: the lawsuit put the 'Caution: Hot' warning on coffee cups

test.source: The verdict, August 18, 1994; trial testimony established that the cup Liebeck held on February 27, 1992 already carried a hot-contents warning, which the jury found too small to read

steps.note: Dated when the claimed cause arrived; tested against the cup in her hands. The warning was already there. Bigger warnings, sturdier lids and lower holding temperatures followed through the 1990s; that is plausible and not documented by any rule.

steps.claim: HBO's Hot Coffee retells the case and the campaign built on it

test.source: Hot Coffee, directed by Susan Saladoff, HBO premiere June 27, 2011 (Sundance, January 2011)

steps.link_why: the film's subject is the case and its use by tort-reform campaigns

title: Columbine, active-shooter doctrine and the lockdown drill (1999)

steps.claim: Two students kill twelve classmates and a teacher at Columbine High School

test.source: Littleton, Colorado, April 20, 1999, 11:19 a.m. to 12:08 p.m.; the first SWAT team entered at 1:09 p.m. and reached the library at 3:22 p.m.

steps.note: On April 20, 1999, two seniors at Columbine High School near Denver shot and killed twelve students and a teacher, wounded more than twenty and then killed themselves. Police followed the doctrine of the day: set a perimeter and wait for SWAT. By the time officers reached the library the shooters had been dead for three hours and a wounded teacher had bled to death. The response, more than the crime, changed how American police and schools prepare for a gunman.

steps.claim: The Million Mom March fills the Mall on Mother's Day

test.source: National Mall, Washington, May 14, 2000; organizers claimed 750,000

steps.link_why: organizer Donna Dees-Thomases dated her decision to the Granada Hills shooting of August 1999; the marchers' speeches and signs were Columbine's

steps.claim: The sheriff's report lays out the timeline, including the 47 minutes before anyone entered the building

test.source: Jefferson County Sheriff's Office, Columbine High School Shootings report, released May 15, 2000

steps.link_why: the official account of the response; its timeline is the basis of every later critique of the perimeter-and-wait doctrine

steps.claim: Colorado voters close the gun-show loophole

test.source: Amendment 22, approved November 7, 2000, 70% to 30%: background checks for all gun-show sales

steps.link_why: the campaign, SAFE Colorado, was founded by Columbine parent Tom Mauser; three of the four guns were bought at a gun show

steps.claim: The Governor's Columbine Review Commission tells police not to wait for SWAT when a gunman is still shooting

test.reason: the report's release in May 2001 that I cannot date to the day

steps.link_why: the Commission's charge was the response to Columbine
steps.note: The Commission (Governor Owens, chaired by William Erickson) recommended that the first officers on scene move toward an active shooter. This is the written start of the doctrine shift in Colorado; it was already being taught in a few departments.

steps.claim: The Secret Service and Department of Education publish the Safe School Initiative, the basis of school threat-assessment teams

test.reason: a federal report published in May 2002 that I cannot date to the day

steps.link_why: the study was commissioned in June 1999 in response to Columbine (its own preface)
steps.note: The study of 37 school attacks found that most attackers had told someone; threat assessment, not profiling, became federal guidance.

steps.claim: ALERRT is founded at Texas State University to train patrol officers to go in

test.reason: a founding in 2002 without a public founding date

steps.link_why: ALERRT's own history states it was created in response to Columbine
wiki: Advanced Law Enforcement Rapid Response Training
steps.note: A partnership of Texas State University, the San Marcos police and the Hays County sheriff; in 2013 the FBI adopted its course as the national standard.

steps.claim: Virginia Tech: a lone gunman kills 32, and the response confirms the solo-officer entry doctrine

test.source: Blacksburg, Virginia, April 16, 2007; the Virginia Tech Review Panel report, August 2007

steps.link_why: the Review Panel measured the police response against post-Columbine doctrine and found it fast; the shooter had chained the doors

steps.claim: Colorado's Claire Davis School Safety Act lets families sue schools that fail to take reasonable care against violence

test.source: Senate Bill 15-213, signed June 3, 2015

steps.link_why: named for the Arapahoe High School shooting of December 13, 2013; its sponsors and the Columbine families who testified for it placed it in Columbine's line

steps.claim: Lockdown drills become standard: 95% of US public schools run them

test.reason: a survey year, not a day; the NCES School Survey on Crime and Safety for 2015–16

steps.link_why: the survey itself; the attribution to Columbine is the schools' own
steps.note: The NCES survey for 2015–16 found 95% of public schools had drilled students on a lockdown procedure. Columbine is where the practice is usually said to begin; the first state mandates came in the 2000s (Illinois, 2005). Plausible and timed, not shown.

title: Flint, the Lead and Copper Rule and the lead-pipe money (2014)

steps.claim: Flint switches its drinking water to the Flint River

test.source: Switch at the Flint water treatment plant, April 25, 2014, under a state-appointed emergency manager; no corrosion control was added

steps.note: Flint, Michigan, a city of about 100,000 under state emergency management, stopped buying Detroit water in April 2014 to save money and drew from the Flint River instead. The river water was more corrosive and the city did not treat it to protect its pipes, so lead leached from old service lines into homes. Officials dismissed complaints for eighteen months. The crisis rewrote the federal lead-in-water rule and put $15 billion into digging up lead pipes nationwide.

steps.claim: General Motors stops using Flint water at its engine plant because it corrodes parts

test.source: GM announcement, October 13, 2014; Flint Township allowed the plant to reconnect to Detroit water

steps.link_why: GM's stated reason was chloride corrosion of engine parts, the same chemistry that was eating the city's pipes

steps.claim: Dr. Mona Hanna-Attisha shows that the share of Flint children with elevated blood lead has doubled

test.source: Hurley Medical Center press conference, September 24, 2015: children under 5 with blood lead ≥5 µg/dL rose from 2.4% to 4.9% after the switch

steps.link_why: her study compared the same clinics before and after April 2014; Virginia Tech's Marc Edwards had reported high lead in tap water on September 8, 2015

steps.claim: Flint switches back to Detroit water

test.source: Reconnection to the Detroit (now Great Lakes Water Authority) system, October 16, 2015

steps.link_why: the state funded the switch two weeks after the blood-lead findings

steps.claim: President Obama declares a federal emergency in Flint

test.source: Federal emergency declaration, January 16, 2016; Governor Snyder had declared a state emergency on January 5, 2016

steps.link_why: the declaration followed the state's request

steps.claim: Claim: Flint prompted the first federal rule on lead in drinking water

test.source: The switch, April 25, 2014; the EPA's Lead and Copper Rule was published June 7, 1991 (56 FR 26460)

steps.note: Dated when the claimed cause arrived; tested against the 1991 rule. The rule was 23 years old; Flint's failure was a failure to follow it (no corrosion control). Busted; what Flint did was force its rewrite.

steps.claim: Michigan adopts the strictest lead rule in the country: all lead service lines out within 20 years

test.source: Michigan Lead and Copper Rule, Mich. Admin. Code R 325.10604f, filed June 14, 2018: action level 12 ppb from 2025, full service-line replacement at utility expense

steps.link_why: Governor Snyder's statement on the rule names Flint; the state's own Flint Water Advisory Task Force (March 2016) recommended it

steps.claim: The EPA's Lead and Copper Rule Revisions require utilities to inventory lead lines and test school water

test.source: Lead and Copper Rule Revisions, 86 FR 4198, published January 15, 2021 (signed December 22, 2020)

steps.link_why: the EPA's rulemaking record and its 2016 'Lead and Copper Rule Revisions White Paper' cite Flint as the reason to reopen the rule

steps.claim: The Bipartisan Infrastructure Law puts $15 billion into replacing lead service lines

test.source: Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, Pub. L. 117-58, signed November 15, 2021

steps.link_why: the White House fact sheet and the floor debate name Flint; Michigan's senators wrote the lead-line provisions

steps.claim: The Lead and Copper Rule Improvements order every lead pipe in the country replaced within ten years

test.source: Lead and Copper Rule Improvements, final rule signed October 8, 2024 (announced in Milwaukee); published 89 FR 86418, October 30, 2024

steps.link_why: the EPA's announcement and the rule's preamble cite Flint; the ten-year clock starts in 2027
